assumptions.summary: The weekday traffic-volume curve is selected as a practical temporal proxy even though the choice is explicitly arbitrary.
Daily traffic is divided evenly between directions in the absence of a reliable directional statistic.
Traffic lights are assumed absent, and sub-capacity drivers are assumed to travel exactly at the speed limit.
Human reaction time is represented by one mean and computer reaction time is approximated as zero.
Autonomous percentage changes the continuum model only by linearly reducing the reaction-time term.
Vehicle arrivals are Poisson and time gaps exponential for light-to-moderate traffic.
Drivers can identify autonomous vehicles and respond to their predictability.
Cooperative vehicles reserve a merge and can create an optimal successful gap.
Finite minimum-gap factors repair the Poisson model in heavy traffic.
All empirical q-u points are assigned to the upper branch until a transition feature can be identified.
Measured flow above the theoretical envelope is handled by lower-bound parameter changes and then a speed clamp.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: A Seattle traffic-sensor daily curve supplies weekday temporal shape.
Car length, zero-speed gap, stopping coefficient, speed limit and reaction time are assembled in Table 1.
Autonomous shares of 0, 10, 50, 90 and 100 percent generate continuum curves.
A cited lane-change time of 4.6 plus or minus 2.3 seconds enters critical-gap geometry.
Continuum outputs at 20, 50 and 80 percent of jam density feed light, moderate and heavy lane simulations.
Average daily traffic counts are scaled by one temporal distribution at every spatial marker.
Thirty-second time intervals and distances between consecutive mile markers define the finite-difference grid.
Empirical maxima drive parameter adjustment and maximum-flow clamping.
Appendix maps retain I-90, I-405 and SR-520 spatial context without adding prose evidence.

The mixed-fleet speed relation feeds the induced-demand derivative.

Gap probabilities and expected waiting feed the three lane cases and heavy-traffic repair.

the Summary exposes three dependent branches: Make a mixed-scale traffic argument auditable before details.
scope is conceded before stakeholder advice: Set confidence before persuasion.
a behavioral mechanism qualifies a technology benefit: Explain how induced traffic can reverse a fixed-density gain.
data granularity and event type select model resolution: Use macroscopic averages and microscopic events for different jobs.
an underdetermined input is openly labeled arbitrary: Keep a practical proxy and its adjustment path visible.
a familiar physical observation precedes notation: Anchor maximal density in following distance before deriving it.
a historical baseline is locally rejected by named defects: Move from literature acknowledgement to a first-principles substitute.
a favorable figure reading refuses an unsupported threshold: Report uniform gains and the absence of clear tipping points.
a favorable result is challenged by induced demand: Use a total derivative to test whether adoption-driven density cancels gains.
interaction cases are narrated before probability formulas: Make actor behavior intelligible before stochastic notation.
an impossible heavy-traffic implication triggers a visible repair: Preserve the useful regime while adding a finite minimum gap.
upstream outputs become downstream shock-wave inputs: Keep cross-model dependencies inspectable.
failed calibration remains in the argument: Show lower-bound tuning, residual mismatch, clamp, and visual artifact.
a spatial interpretation is explicitly marked non-rigorous: Separate a suggestive location from a verified interchange.
sensitivity is read through direction and boundary: Connect parameter changes to physical intuition and divergence.
strengths and weaknesses are separated by model branch: Tie each capability and defect to its consequence.
stronger temporal evidence narrows a policy window: Recommend peak-period action when time structure is clearer than space structure.
an intentional simplification is called unrealistic: Expose the safe-driver premise and why it is retained.
specific lane-change readings feed a conditional action: Translate wait and gap changes into an operational recommendation.
a concrete limitation names the next data or model repair: Turn a failed condition into future work.

results_trace.summary: At fixed density, flow and mean speed increase fairly uniformly as autonomous share rises; no clear tipping point appears.
The total derivative is negative for the modeled induced-density changes when autonomous fraction is below one.
From Case 1 to 2 in light traffic, acceptable-gap probability rises 170 percent, wait falls from 23.27 to 8.61 seconds, and minimum merge distance falls to 37 percent.
Moderate traffic gives a 204 percent probability increase and waiting/minimum distance near one third of the original values.
The conventional light-traffic shock-wave example reports temporary flow at 31.36 percent, density at 200.11 percent, and a 0.30-mile queue involving 26.7 vehicles.
Empirical traffic flow remains above the theoretical envelope after lower-bound parameter adjustment, so the source clamps speed at the theoretical maximum-flow point.
Temporal source-flux structure is more decisive than spatial inference and motivates a rush-hour-only designated-lane suggestion.
Sensitivity directions broadly match physical intuition, while zero total spacing yields an infinite-density boundary.

source.title: Driving Towards the Future: Modeling the Impact of Driverless Vehicles on Traffic Patterns

source_quality.summary: All 29 physical pages were read and visually reviewed. The paper moves from a physically motivated continuum model to discrete lane-change cases and shock waves, then preserves the empirical overflow, lower-bound retuning, maximum-flow clamp and resulting visual discontinuities before a conditional policy handoff.

decisions: which modeling resolution fits each phenomenon, how autonomous share changes capacity, whether added vehicles erase the benefit, how lane cooperation changes merge delay, how to handle empirical overflow, and when a designated lane is defensible

title: Driving Towards the Future: Modeling the Impact of Driverless Vehicles on Traffic Patterns
unresolved_questions: The weekday curve is selected arbitrarily from two curves consistent with the peak-hour statement.
Traffic is split evenly by direction without a reliable directional statistic.
Traffic lights are assumed absent because data could not be found.
The safe-driver premise fixes all sub-capacity vehicles at exactly the speed limit and is openly unrealistic.
Computer reaction time is approximated as zero and human reaction time as a single mean.
Stopping distance is interpolated from only zero and 60 mph and ignores vehicle and road heterogeneity.
Autonomous share only linearly scales reaction time and omits mixed interaction and cooperation effects.
First-principles motivation does not establish predictive accuracy over empirical alternatives.
The induced-demand derivative approximates finite density and fleet changes and assumes added cars are driverless.
No tipping point in selected curves is weaker than proving that no equilibrium or threshold exists.
Poisson arrivals and exponential gaps are asserted for light-to-moderate traffic without a fitted diagnostic.
The source's lambda/mu notation is inconsistent or text-corrupted and needs a unit-checked definition.
Critical gap is calculated from physics although the source later admits its definition calls for empirical data.
Lane-change time 4.6 plus or minus 2.3 seconds has large uncertainty that is not propagated.
Case 2 assumes drivers can identify autonomous vehicles and adjust trust predictably.
Case 3 assumes reservations, optimal coordination, and that any gap can be made successful.
Heavy-traffic corrections use uncalibrated one-third and one-half factors.
Shock-wave calculations assume instantaneous change and a new constant uniform speed.
The claim that Cases 2 and 3 avoid all queue effects is stronger than the idealized simulation supports.
One universal daily temporal distribution is applied at every highway location.
The noninvertible flow-speed relation is forced onto the upper branch without a data-based state classifier.
Empirical flow exceeds theory, parameter tuning uses the same evidence, and a clamp is then imposed.
Discontinuities in source-flux outputs are artifacts of the maximum-flow clamp.
Possible interchange locations are inferred without rigorous spatial analysis.
One-at-a-time sensitivity includes degenerate zero-spacing cases and omits interactions and uncertainty distributions.
Finite-difference error is acknowledged but not quantified against time and space refinement.
One highway segment and internal appendix plots do not support region-wide generalization.
The designated-lane recommendation lacks capacity, compliance, equity, induced-demand, and implementation analysis.
No executable code, solver stencil, frozen raw data, parameter-fit trace, or uncertainty propagation is released.
